title: Region funds A Better Tent City transition
subtitle: Reporting safeguards added, Cambridge equity concerns raised, delegates object to visitor limits and operator change.
overview: Regional Council approved a plan to bring A Better Tent City into the formal housing stability system, with The Working Centre as operator {{vote:m1}}. The site's volunteer board is dissolving. Without a regional plan, the people living there would face a wind-down, and the Waterloo District School Board and City of Kitchener, as the site's owners, would decide its future. Staff said about 55 people live there.

The plan adds $2.50M in capital funding and $2.56M in 2026 operating funding from reserves, with no 2026 levy impact. It also adds three staff positions. Council attached an amendment {{vote:m3}} requiring regular reports to the Community and Health Services Committee on spending, housing outcomes and site compliance. It also says any 2027 funding must go through the normal budget process and is not automatic.

Many delegates opposed the changes, including limits on visitors and the shift to a new operator. Some councillors worried about cost and Cambridge's unmet needs. A proposal on equity and Cambridge investment was withdrawn and is expected to return separately.

decisions.detail: Council approved the A Better Tent City Stabilization and Transition Plan and its funding as set out in report CSD-HOU-26-003 {{vote:m1}}.
The 2025 Housing Services capital program was increased by $2.50M, financed through reserves.
The 2026 Housing Services operating budget was increased by $2.56M, financed through reserves with no regional levy impact.
Council approved adding one Support Worker and two Program Analyst positions in 2026 to provide housing support.

Staff must report regularly to the Community and Health Services Committee on spending, housing outcomes, site compliance and ways to offset 2027 costs, and any 2027 funding must go through the regular budget process {{vote:m3}}.

An amendment supporting the site in principle and asking for an equity impact assessment and a Cambridge investment strategy was withdrawn by unanimous consent, with the themes to return at a later meeting.

debate: Delegates opposed the plan over its rules: no visitors, limits on kitchen use, cabin checks and no staff living on site. They said these would undo the community and autonomy that defined the site. Some asked that another organization operate it, and others said residents and the founder had not been consulted.

The board chair supported the plan and said the site's board approached the Region, which then approached The Working Centre. A delegate said there are fewer visitor options than before and that the end of visitor access would leave a gap, especially for people who drop in for meals, showers and laundry.

One councillor argued Cambridge is underserved, citing warming-centre overcapacity and a women's shelter turning people away, and wanted money redirected there. Staff advised that cutting the budget was too risky because the Region would be legally responsible for the site. They said the community-based funding would be used across the region.

Several councillors said the cost and its effect on the 2027 budget were concerns, and some preferred permanent supportive housing over transitional shelter. Others supported the plan because people live there now and no cheaper option was available. Supporters said the added reporting and the no-automatic-funding clause made it acceptable.

Councillors also debated procedure: some objected to amendments being handed out mid-meeting, especially for colleagues with low vision. Others said discussion legitimately prompts changes and that preparing in advance is hard around other work.
